sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. The model keeps every Gaussian valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so mesh can be derived at any time from field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussians initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io 1. Introduction Capturing dynamic scene, person in motion, mechanism at work, or an animal on the move, and turning it into digital asset is the first step toward bringing the physical world into the virtual world. It is long-standing goal of computer vision and graphics, and recent progress in novelview synthesis has brought it within reach. Neural radiance fields [47] first reconstructed static scenes from photographs with striking realism, and 3D Gaussian splatting [28] has since made it fast enough to become the representation of choice. Dynamic variants of Gaussian splatting bring this to videos, allowing immersive rendering of the scene from novel views and camera trajectories. However, these dynamic methods optimize for appearance, and the surfaces extracted from them are often noisy and incomplete. This 1 matters for downstream applications that need accurate perframe geometry, like physical interaction with virtual objects, relighting, and AR/VR scene composition. Current dynamic Gaussian methods, whether built on deformation fields [70, 73], 4D primitives [74], sparse control points [25], or per-Gaussian trajectories [37, 42, 62, 68], encode appearance and motion but do not have representation of the surface, either implicit or explicit. To reconstruct the scenes surfaces, volume has to be built from the trained model after the fact, by TSDF volume integration [14] on depth maps rendered from many viewpoints and passed to marching cubes [41] on fixed-resolution grid. Since the optimization constrains geometry only through appearance, the models carry many floaters, which distort the input volumes of the marching cubes and lead to noisy reconstructions. For static scenes, this problem has been addressed by training Gaussians to represent geometry alongside appearance. One family of methods regularizes the Gaussians so that their rendered depth, and hence its fusion, is accurate [10, 24, 80]. second family defines field directly from the Gaussians and extracts its level set with marching tetrahedra [21, 23, 55, 79], which removes depth fusion altogether and adapts the mesh resolution to the Gaussians. For dynamic scenes, the few methods that reconstruct surfaces [39, 71, 83] are object-centric, relying on foreground masks to isolate single object, and remain slow to train. In this work, we aim to bring the field-based extraction of the second family to complete, unmasked dynamic scenes captured by multiple synchronized cameras, allowing the full scene geometry to be extracted at every frame. We build on three key insights. First, every Gaussian must remain valid surface element at every frame of the sequence. Second, the model should carry an implicit representation of the scenes dynamic geometry. Third, training struggles to recover large and fast motion without good starting point. To realize the first two insights, we propose per-Gaussian temporal motion model that represents each Gaussians changes in position and rotation over time as linear combination of temporal Gaussian kernels, inspired by radial basis function (RBF) networks [5, 49] and Gaussian processes (GPs) [56]. To realize the third, we introduce track-based initialization scheme that assigns each initial Gaussian trajectory consistent with the observed motion. Since the temporal Gaussian kernels span the whole timeline, each Gaussian can follow complex motion and remains valid surface element throughout the sequence. It can therefore carry an implicit representation of the surface, such as oriented normals [21], along its trajectory. Polynomial trajectories [37, 68], in contrast, hold only within short time windows and introduce geometric noise outside them. Since each trajectory is linear in its kernel weights, our initialization scheme fits it in closed form by GP regression to point tracks spanning the whole sequence, so even large and fast motion is captured from the start. With our model, the surface is defined at any time, and mesh follows at every frame from marching tetrahedra, with no depth rendering or fusion  (Fig. 1)  . Evaluating dynamic geometry requires ground-truth meshes that evolve with the scene, and no public dataset pairs synchronized multi-camera captures with exact timevarying geometry. We therefore build Blender-Moments, benchmark of nine animated scenes, rendered from multiple synchronized cameras, whose ground-truth meshes can be extracted at any frame. We evaluate our method on this new dataset and on two existing real-world datasets, Neural 3D Video [34] and SelfCap [72], and compare it to state-of-theart dynamic methods, including ones designed for surface reconstruction. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate dynamic geometry, and its novel-view synthesis rivals that of the strongest baselines. Its advantage is largest on scenes with large and fast motion. It also trains in time comparable to the fastest dynamic splatting methods. In summary, our contributions are: framework for joint appearance and per-frame mesh reconstruction of complete dynamic scenes, achieving stateof-the-art surface reconstruction. novel motion model and initialization technique inspired by Gaussian processes. multi-view benchmark for dynamic surface reconstruction, with ground-truth meshes at every frame. 2. Related Work Static scenes. Novel-view synthesis methods such as neural radiance fields [47] and 3D Gaussian splatting [28] are optimized for appearance alone and do not model the scenes geometry. Many works have addressed this by extending these representations to recover surfaces. For radiance fields, several works [36, 64, 67, 76] map an implicit surface representation to volume density, so that volume rendering recovers the surface together with appearance. For Gaussians, two classes of methods have emerged. The first regularizes the Gaussians so that their rendered depth is accurate, and extracts meshes by TSDF volume integration of that depth. 2DGS [24] pioneered this class by flattening the Gaussians into 2D surfels with well-defined normals. Later works adopt planar [10] or quadratic [85] primitives, rasterize depth and normals in closed form [80], supervise normals with monocular priors [13], or treat Gaussians as stochastic solids [81]. The second class defines field directly from the Gaussians and extracts its level set with marching tetrahedra on Delaunay tetrahedralization of Gaussian-derived points. GOF [79] introduced this approach with an opacity field, which SOF [55] evaluates faster by sorting the Gaussians along each ray. MILo [23] learns signed distances at nine pivots per Gaussian and extracts mesh during training, whose rendered depth and normals regularize the Gaussians. 2 Gaussian Wrapping [21] treats each Gaussian as an oriented surface element whose vacancy field yields detailed meshes. Other works jointly optimize the Gaussians with neural signed [12, 43, 77, 84] or unsigned [33] distance field, or align the Gaussians with the surface and reconstruct mesh by Poisson reconstruction [22]. All of these methods assume static scene. Dynamic scenes. Both radiance fields and Gaussian splatting have been extended from static to dynamic scenes. For radiance fields, common approach [51, 52, 54, 61] is to warp rays into canonical space with learned deformation field. Other works condition the field on time [34, 40] or factorize it into space-time feature planes [8, 20]. For Gaussians, 4DGS [70] and Deformable-3DGS [73] carry over the canonical-deformation approach [51, 52, 54, 61], and many later methods follow it [4, 38, 88]. Other methods drive the Gaussians by blending the rigid motions of sparse set of control nodes [25, 32, 65]. Another line of works models per-Gaussian motion explicitly. Dynamic3DGS [42] pioneered this direction, storing each Gaussians position and rotation at every frame. Later methods make this motion more compact and expressive, either with Gaussians whose position and opacity vary over time [16, 37, 68, 72, 74], or by parameterizing each trajectory with keyframes, splines, or other temporal bases [27, 31, 50, 62]. The methods above are trained for appearance alone, with no dedicated representation of the surface. Dynamic surface reconstruction methods initially addressed this with neural implicit surfaces that deform or evolve signed distance function over time [6, 17, 45, 59, 67, 75]. More recently, Gaussian-based dynamic surface reconstruction methods have emerged, in three forms. Hybrid NeRFGaussian methods [29, 35] couple dynamic Gaussians with volumerendered signed distance function. Hybrid meshGaussian methods [44, 60, 87] bind Gaussians to an input mesh that they deform or track over time. Lastly, Gaussian-only methods [7, 11, 39, 66, 71, 83] represent the surface with oriented or flattened Gaussians and extract each frames mesh by volume integration of rendered depth or by Poisson reconstruction. Across all three groups, most methods target isolated objects with foreground masks and rely on bounded volumetric grids or input meshes to recover the surface, which keeps them from reconstructing complete dynamic scenes. 3. Method Given multi-view videos of dynamic scene captured by synchronized and calibrated cameras, MEMO reconstructs persistent oriented Gaussians whose geometry is defined at every time [0, 1]. Geometry is represented with the oriented normals proposed in Gaussian Wrapping [21], and our motion model computes each Gaussians position, rotation, and normal at any time (Sec. 4.1). Before training, we initialize each Gaussians trajectory by fitting its motion model to point tracks spanning the sequence (Sec. 4.2). Training then optimizes all parameters with photometric and geometric losses (Sec. 4.3). After training, mesh can be extracted directly at any frame with marching tetrahedra on the Gaussians evaluated at that time. An overview of our full pipeline is shown in Fig. 2. 4.1. Motion Model MEMO attaches temporal model to every Gaussian, encoding motion as displacements from base position and rotation at each query time t. Assuming locally rigid motion, the scale of each Gaussian stays constant. The displacements are modeled as linear combination of temporal Gaussian kernels, where each kernel is centered around different inducing time. Since the kernels cover the whole timeline, the model holds at every frame, so opacity can remain constant as well. This ensures that every Gaussian remains active at every frame, whereas prior works vary opacity over time [16, 37, 68, 72, 74] because their motion models hold only within short windows. Mesh extraction. At inference, we evaluate the motion model at frame to get the state of the Gaussians, and extract the frames mesh following the pivot-based method of Gaussian Wrapping. We spawn two pivots from each Gaussian and compute the Delaunay tetrahedralization of all pivots. We evaluate the vacancy field at the pivots and extract its 0.5 isosurface with marching tetrahedra. 4.2. Initialization Dynamic scenes often contain large and fast motion, such as swinging limbs or spinning parts. Such motion is challenging for any motion model, since photometric gradients only guide Gaussian toward nearby image content. One way to mitigate this challenge is to start from good initial approximation of the motion. Most prior methods, however, forgo this approach and start from static model [39, 70, 73] or from zero motion [25, 62, 83]. Others approximate the motion only between consecutive frames [42, 68], where large displacements can divert trajectories. Our initialization scheme instead finds for each Gaussian Gi 3D trajectory spanning the entire sequence, using closed-form fit to tracks built from per-frame SfM points, so that large and fast motion is captured before training begins. Our initialization runs once before training and takes as input sparse COLMAP [58] point cloud at every frame, as in [37, 68]. First, we link these points into 3D tracks over the entire sequence. We begin by selecting one or more anchor frames according to the scene. single anchor at the first or middle frame suffices when the moving content is visible there, whereas scenes whose content is revealed over time use several anchors spread across the sequence. Since every anchor starts new track for each of its points, including static ones, scenes dominated by static background use few anchors. From each anchor, Kalman filter [26] then runs forward and backward through the sequence, associating each point with the nearest point to its predicted position. 5 Figure 4. 200 sampled tracks of Lego from our initialization with single first-frame anchor, over the first-frame mesh. The fitted trajectories follow the bucket through its full sweep before training begins. Dots are track positions every tenth frame, and curves of the same color are the fitted trajectories. Implausible matches are rejected with Mahalanobis gate, in which case the track follows the motion of its nearest accepted neighbors instead of being diverted. The tracks of all anchors are united. Second, we fit the position weights of each Gaussian to its track in closed form by GP regression [56], with the inducing times and lengthscales fixed at the bin centers and the bin width, respectively, and set its rotation deltas to the identity quaternion. Finally, if the tracks yield fewer than 50K Gaussians, we densify the initialization by sampling additional Gaussians uniformly within shell around the tracked points. Each spawned Gaussian inherits the motion weights of its nearest tracked Gaussian. Figure 4 shows the Kalman tracks and the trajectories fitted to them. 4.3. Experiments 5.1. Experimental Setup Datasets. Evaluating dynamic surface reconstruction requires ground-truth geometry. To that end, we introduce Blender-Moments, benchmark of nine animated scenes rendered in Blender (Fig. S6), from articulated machinery to deforming animals and characters, each 100 to 170 frames long. Every frame is rendered from 50 training and 10 test cameras around the scene, and ground-truth mesh can be exported from the animation at any frame. While DGMesh [39] also provides ground-truth meshes, it is singleview dataset, outside the scope of our multi-view setting. To demonstrate the robustness of MEMO on real footage, we complement Blender-Moments with six scenes of Neural 3D Video [34] and seven scenes of SelfCap [72]. GS [25], FreeTimeGS [68], and AST-3DGS [62], and two geometry-based dynamic methods, D-2DGS [83] and DGMesh [39]. For all baselines except DG-Mesh, we extract meshes by TSDF fusion [14] of the rendered depth maps. DG-Mesh instead relies on differentiable Poisson reconstruction [53] during both training and inference. This restricts DG-Mesh to bounded foreground objects and rules out the real scenes, so we evaluate it on Blender-Moments only. Metrics. We evaluate novel-view synthesis, geometry, and runtime. For novel-view synthesis, we report PSNR, SSIM [69], and LPIPS [82] on the held-out views of all datasets. For geometry, we compare meshes qualitatively on all datasets and quantitatively on Blender-Moments. In each Blender-Moments scene, we extract ground-truth meshes at ten evenly spaced frames. We measure position with the Chamfer distance and orientation with the normal Chamfer distance [46], but neither suffices alone. Point distances barely penalize surface noise, so noisy mesh can outscore clean one, while normal angles can miss significant surface offset. Our primary metric is therefore joint F-score, which requires matched points to agree both in position (distance within 1% of the scenes bounding-box diagonal) and in orientation (normals within 20). We compute the normal metrics both on surface samples and on normals rendered at the test views. For runtime, we report training time. For fairness, all methods run on single NVIDIA A100 GPU with 80GB of VRAM. 5.2. Results & Comparisons Baselines. We compare against five dynamic Gaussian splatting methods, 4DGS [70], Deformable-3DGS [73], SCWe compare MEMO with the baselines in geometry, novelview synthesis, and efficiency, and ablate its components. 6 Deformable-3DGS DG-Mesh D-2DGS MEMO Ground truth L h E y n a a g Deformable-3DGS D-2DGS MEMO Figure 5. Meshes of MEMO and the baselines, rendered from novel viewpoints. The top rows show three Blender-Moments scenes beside the ground truth, and the bottom rows show the real scenes Flame salmon and Yoga, with each methods color render inset and the crop outlined in red. Deformable-3DGS represents the appearance-only methods, as its meshes look the best among them, and the gray dots are Gaussian floaters. MEMO produces clean surfaces and preserves fine details such as facial features and Lego studs, where D-2DGS leaves noise and holes and DG-Mesh oversmooths. D-2DGS fails on Yoga, as its render shows. The supplement adds per-scene results, mesh comparisons with all baselines, and the complete ablation study. Geometry. MEMO reconstructs the cleanest meshes  (Fig. 5)  , and on Blender-Moments, where ground-truth geometry is available, they also score best in normal accuracy and joint F-score (Tab. 1a). Across all methods, the joint F-score agrees with the visual quality of the meshes, whereas the Chamfer distance barely penalizes their noise. Both the representation and its extraction account for our lead. Meshed by TSDF fusion, MEMO still surpasses every baseline in normal accuracy and joint F-score. Marching tetrahedra on the vacancy field improves on both TSDF fusion and Poisson reconstruction. This advantage comes from sampling the field at the Gaussians, which follow the geometry, so the mesh has an adaptive resolution that is finer where the surface has more detail. In contrast, TSDF fusion and Poisson reconstruction solve on fixed grid, where finer detail requires finer grid everywhere and thus larger, more complex meshes. Poisson reconstruction further oversmooths the surface and requires watertight, segmented objects, as our meshes reconstructed by Poisson show (Tab. 1a). Novel-view synthesis. Our representation of geometry does not come at the cost of appearance. On every dataset, MEMO performs comparably to the dynamic splatting methods that model appearance only, and it renders the best novel views on Blender-Moments and the best PSNR and SSIM on SelfCap (Tab. 1a). It also keeps fast-moving parts sharp where other methods blur them  (Fig. 6)  . Unlike our method, the other two geometry-based methods lose image quality (Tab. 1a). DG-Mesh [39] renders far below every other method, and the quality of D-2DGS [83] does not translate from Blender-Moments to the real scenes. Efficiency. Table 2 summarizes our ablations, removing one component of MEMO at time, and Sec. reports the complete study. Without the trajectory fit, the real scenes lose their fast-moving parts, although their PSNR is nearly unchanged due to the static background (Fig. S3). On the synthetic scenes, which have no background, the damage shows in every metric and grows as the motion gets larger and faster (Tab. S2d). Halving the kernel count or removing the boundary inducing times also degrades appearance and geometry. 6. Discussion Limitations. Although MEMO recovers accurate meshes of complete dynamic scenes, it has several limitations. First, 8 it extracts each frames mesh independently, so consecutive meshes are not guaranteed to share vertices or faces, and extracting temporally consistent meshes remains future work. Second, its motion relies on the initial tracks, so thin, fastmoving parts that the tracker misses can be smeared or lost. Third, since every Gaussian stores its own motion, its model is the largest among the compared methods. Finally, like other methods that reconstruct geometry from images, it is affected by the ambiguity between albedo and shading and by narrow camera baselines, which can leave reliefs in the mesh or weakly constrained depth. Section discusses these limitations in depth, and Fig. S1 illustrates its failure cases. Conclusion. We presented MEMO, which jointly reconstructs the appearance and geometry of complete dynamic scenes. Its per-Gaussian temporal motion model represents each Gaussians motion over the whole sequence, so its geometry is defined at every frame. track-based initialization further lets it recover large and fast motion. We also introduced Blender-Moments, multi-view benchmark with ground-truth meshes at every frame. MEMO extracts the most accurate per-frame meshes while keeping novel-view synthesis and training time on par with the strongest dynamic splatting methods.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, as coding and writing assistant. In the research, it assisted with implementing and debugging the method, the evaluation infrastructure, and the figure scripts. It also assisted with analyzing experimental results, discussing design alternatives, and surveying related work. In the writing, it drafted and edited text, and assisted with the bibliography. All use was directed and approved by the authors, who reviewed and verified all LLM-assisted code and text. All research ideas, design decisions, experiments, and claims are the authors.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: This supplementary material complements the main paper. Section discusses the limitations of MEMO. Section details its implementation, including the extension of its static components to dynamic scenes, and Sec. ablates its components. Section describes Blender-Moments, the inputs shared by all methods, and the evaluation protocol, and Sec. reports additional results, including per-scene metrics and further comparisons. Videos of all scenes, comparing our method with every baseline, are available on https: //memo-4d.github.io/comparisons.html. A. Limitations Per-frame extraction. MEMO extracts the mesh of each frame independently, so consecutive meshes are not guaranteed to share vertices or faces. This has two causes, the lack of single tetrahedralization that stays valid over the whole sequence, and the vacancy field, which changes over time. As the Gaussians move and rotate, their pivots shift and the structure of the tetrahedralization changes with them, especially under articulated motion and for parts hidden during part of the sequence, such as the pages of Book or the engine bay of Toyota. Even if stable tetrahedralization existed, the time-varying vacancy field would change which edges its 0.5 level set crosses, and with them the output of marching tetrahedra. Extracting temporally consistent meshes is left for future work. Motion recovery of thin, fast-moving parts. Thin, fastmoving parts are hard to track, and the initialization of MEMO (Sec. 4.2) may miss them. Training then struggles to recover their motion, since Gaussian receives gradients only from the pixels it covers. Without good initial track, thin part that moves far between frames has either no Gaussians or static Gaussians. In the latter case, the Gaussians match the part in single frame, but in the others they occlude what lies behind them and increase the rendering error, so training lowers their opacity. Either way, the part is smeared or lost. Figure S1a shows two instances, the rotating knob of Lego and the spinning wheel spokes of Bicycle. Albedo and shading ambiguity. As with other methods that reconstruct geometry from appearance, MEMO faces the ambiguity between albedo and shading. Sharp appearance boundaries, whether from lighting or from texture, can leave relief in the mesh, as shown in Fig. S1b. Using multiple viewpoints per frame keeps the ambiguity to minimum. Narrow camera baselines. narrow, front-facing camera rig, as in Neural 3D Video [34], sees surfaces parallel to its image planes with little parallax, which can leave their depth weakly constrained. Such surface can then be displaced toward the cameras while still rendering correctly from the training views, as shown in Fig. S1c. Model size. MEMO has the largest models among the compared methods, on average 46% larger than those of FreeTimeGS [68], the second largest. Although MEMO uses about 3 times fewer Gaussians than FreeTimeGS, each of its Gaussians stores about 4 times more parameters. Fixing the inducing times and lengthscales at their initial values reduces the memory footprint by 18 to 20% at cost of up to 0.6 dB in PSNR. Adapting the number of kernels to each Gaussians motion, as AST-3DGS [62] does with its keyframes, would reduce it further, and we leave it to future work. B. Implementation Details B.1. Lifting static components to 4D Three components of MEMO come from methods for static scenes, the importance-based densification and simplification of Mini-Splatting2 [19], the 3D filter of MipSplatting [78], and the normal-error densification of Gaussian Wrapping [21]. Each relies on its own sweep over all the training views, which accumulates per-Gaussian statistics. naive extension to dynamic scenes would be to sweep over every training view at every frame. However, this is time-consuming and largely redundant, since neighboring Gaussians move coherently and their relative arrangement changes little between consecutive frames. Instead, we set budget of views per sweep (Tab. S1). If full sweep over training views and frames exceeds it, the sweep renders the training views of every K-th frame only, with = /N . Below, we briefly review each component and describe how we lift it to 4D. Mini-Splatting2. Mini-Splatting2 [19] complements the gradient-based densification of 3DGS [28] with an importance-based pipeline. The importance of Gaussian is its accumulated blending weight across all the training views. The pipeline densifies the scene by cloning the most important Gaussians while pruning negligible ones (aggressive cloning), and later simplifies it in two events that prune the least important Gaussians. Since aggressive cloning densifies the scene much faster, densification ends at iteration 3K instead of 15K. During training, Mini-Splatting2 also reinitializes the Gaussians from points sampled on the rendered depth, which removes floaters and Gaussians hidden behind surfaces. To lift Mini-Splatting2 to 4D, we accumulate importance separately for each sampled frame. Both the cloning and the simplification events prune Gaussian only if it is unimportant in every sampled frame. Gaussians visible in only few frames, such as parts hidden during most of the sequence, therefore survive pruning. We drop the depth reinitialization, since replacing the Gaussians would discard their trajectories. 3D mip filter. Mip-Splatting [78] prevents aliasing by ensuring that each Gaussian is at least as large as pixel of the training views that see it. It convolves each Gaussian 14 with an isotropic Gaussian kernel the size of pixel at the closest of these views, and scales the opacity down so that the total contribution of each Gaussian is preserved. This size is determined by the Gaussians distance to the cameras, which varies from frame to frame in dynamic scene. To lift the filter to 4D, we determine each Gaussians kernel size from its closest distance to the training views over the whole sequence, according to its position at each sampled frame. As in Mip-Splatting, we recompute the filter whenever Gaussians are added or removed, and periodically after densification to account for the optimization updates. Since each recomputation evaluates the motion model at every sampled frame, we increase the period from 100 to 1K iterations to reduce training time. Normal-error densification. Normal-error densification was proposed in Gaussian Wrapping [21] to close holes in the surfaces. For each Gaussian, it accumulates the error between its oriented normal and the normal of the rendered depth across the training views. The Gaussians with the largest error are then cloned with flipped normals, so that either orientation can be kept. To lift normal-error densification to 4D, we accumulate each Gaussians error over all the sampled frames. B.2. Mesh extraction To extract the mesh at time t, we first apply the motion model and obtain each Gaussians position, rotation, and oriented normal at t. Then, we follow the two-pivot mesh extraction pipeline of Gaussian Wrapping [21]. Each Gaussian contributes two pivots, its center and the point three standard deviations from it along its oriented normal. The pivots are tetrahedralized with GPU Delaunay triangulation [9]. Next, we evaluate the vacancy at each pivot from the training views captured at t. Finally, we extract the mesh as the 0.5 level set of the vacancy with marching tetrahedra. After extraction, we clean the mesh using the following steps: We remove faces with vertex farther from the center of the camera rig than five times its radius. We remove faces with an edge longer than 0.2 times the rig radius. We remove connected components of fewer than 5,000 faces. We remove faces whose barycenter vacancy exceeds the 99th percentile over all faces. This removes faces that marching tetrahedra places across empty space, for example between two nearby parts or across depth edge. By default, the vacancy is evaluated with the 3D mip filter on, which attenuates the Gaussians opacity. This attenuation can affect thin structures, whose Gaussians become nearly transparent, so that the vacancy around them stays just above 0.5 and removes them from the mesh. We therefore add an opt-in thin-structures mode that evaluates the vacancy with the unattenuated opacities and keeps thin structures intact. Evaluation protocol We evaluate all methods with the same protocol. We measure the image quality of the test views on all datasets, the mesh quality on Blender-Moments, the only dataset with groundtruth meshes, and the training time. For image quality, we compute PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS with VGG backbone on every frame of every test camera, and average them over all test images. The training time is the wall-clock time of training on single 80GB NVIDIA A100 GPU. For mesh quality, we compare each methods mesh with the ground-truth mesh at the ten evaluated frames of every Blender-Moments scene, and average the metrics over them. We measure position accuracy with the point Chamfer distance between 200K points sampled uniformly over each meshs surface, normalized by the diagonal of the groundtruth bounding box. Point distances barely penalize surface noise. noisy surface that oscillates around the ground truth stays close to it everywhere, so it can outscore clean surface with small offset. Surface noise, however, does affect the normals. We therefore complement the traditional Chamfer distance with the normal Chamfer distance [46], which averages the angle between the normals of nearest samples on the two meshes. Conversely, normal angles ignore surface offsets. surface displaced far from the ground truth, but parallel to it, keeps its normals and still scores perfectly. The two Chamfer distances can rank methods in opposite orders. One method may have lower point Chamfer distance but higher normal Chamfer distance than another. Taken separately, the two scores cannot determine which of the two methods produces higher-quality meshes. We therefore define joint F-score, and compute its precision and recall with the following condition. sample and its nearest sample on the other mesh form correct match when their distance is below 1% of the diagonal and their normals differ by less than 20. Across all methods, the joint F-score agrees with the visual quality of the meshes more consistently than either the point or the normal Chamfer distance alone (Sec. 5.2), and we therefore use it as our primary geometry metric. For completeness, we also compute the joint F-score on rendered normals, defined on image pixels instead of 3D nearest neighbors, which scores only the parts of the surface visible from the test views. At every test camera of an evaluated frame, we rasterize both meshes with nvdiffrast [30] and apply the same match condition to the depths and normals of each pixel. Lastly, on SelfCap [72], all methods need one postprocessing step before evaluation. The SelfCap cameras stand on half-circle rig, so parts of the rig appear in the views of the cameras facing them. Every method reconstructs these parts with floaters near the cameras, which can occlude novel views. We therefore remove from every methods model, after training, the Gaussians that lie within 15% of the scene extent from training camera and inside its frustum. At inference, we do the same for every novel-view camera. E. Additional Results This section reports additional results.
